notes: Slot 4 = Communist Party of Tajikistan (Rasulov), MD CPT sprite kept as the same party. Leninabad clan in 13, Hindustani's underground hujra in 14 (traditionalist, apolitical), young Said Abdullo Nuri's circle in 12, radical hujra students in 11, SADUM qaziyat in 10, Pamiri Ismailis in 8/9, 201st MRD (Dushanbe) in 22, Manghit dynasty of Bukhara in 23.

0.name: Muhojironi Bukhoro
0.text:
The Bukharan Émigrés are the merchants, clerics and notables who fled the Red Army's conquest of Bukhara in 1920 and the defeat of the Basmachi, settling in Peshawar, Karachi, Kabul, Jeddah and Istanbul. By 1970 their sons are prosperous traders, bound by marriage and memory to the lost cities of the emirate.

They hope for a liberated, authoritarian and Islamic Central Asia, and pin their hopes on Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and ultimately the United States as the enemies of Moscow. They have no army and little contact with the Tajik SSR. Their leverage is money, pilgrim networks to Mecca and access to anti-communist governments.

1.name: Merosi Somoniyon
1.text:
The Samanid Heritage school unites historians, orientalists and teachers around Bobojon Ghafurov, former First Secretary of the republic and since 1956 director of the Institute of Oriental Studies in Moscow, who is writing a grand history of the Tajiks. They present the Samanid state of the tenth century as the golden age of the nation.

They stand for continuity with the Persian classical tradition, pride in Rudaki and Avicenna, respect for family and learning, and a Tajik identity distinct from the Turkic world. They remain loyal Soviet scholars and avoid confrontation. Their leverage is Ghafurov's prestige in Moscow, the Academy of Sciences and the school curriculum.

2.name: Nasli shastum
2.text:
The Sixties Generation are the young Tajik poets and writers of the Thaw, among them Loiq Sherali and Bozor Sobir, who broke with the stiff verse of socialist realism and returned to the language of Hafez and Rumi. In 1970 they publish in Dushanbe journals, read before packed halls and are watched warily by the censors.

They want freedom of expression, honest treatment of the past, the restoration of Persian as a living literary language and a culture open to the wider Persian world. They avoid open dissent and any link to the West. Their leverage is the enormous popularity of poetry and the admiration of students across the republic.

3.name: Shuroi ittifoqhoi kasabai Tojikiston
3.english: Tajik Republican Council of Trade Unions
3.text:
The Tajik Republican Council of Trade Unions is the republican branch of the All-Union Central Council of Trade Unions, organising textile workers, miners, builders and state-farm labourers from Leninabad to Kurgan-Tyube. In 1970 it remains a transmission belt of the party, but it distributes housing, holidays and social insurance to hundreds of thousands.

Within those limits it presses for better wages, safer workplaces, kindergartens and housing in the fast-growing towns, and for a fair share of jobs for Tajiks in industry. It supports the Soviet order and its foreign policy. Its leverage lies in the factory committees and in the welfare network on which workers' families depend.

4.name: Hizbi Kommunistii Tojikiston
4.text:
The Communist Party of Tajikistan is the republican branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and the only legal party of the Tajik SSR. Since 1961 it has been led by First Secretary Jabbor Rasulov, an agronomist from the Leninabad region and a cautious, dependable ally of Leonid Brezhnev.

The party drives cotton production, the construction of the Nurek dam and the education of a Tajik professional class, while balancing the rival regions of the republic. It is loyal to Moscow, hostile to the United States and wary of China and of religious revival across the Afghan border. Its power rests on the nomenklatura and the Leninabad cadres around Rasulov.

5.name: Sozandagoni Norak
5.text:
The Nurek Builders are the Komsomol volunteers, tunnellers and engineers from across the Union who are raising the world's tallest earth-fill dam on the Vakhsh river. Their settlement at Nurek is a frontier town of barracks, brigades and slogans, where young workers feel they are building communism with their own hands.

They are radical egalitarians who want the brigades to run the work, equal pay, an end to managerial privilege and the idealism of the revolution renewed. They distrust bureaucrats more than any foreign power. Their leverage is that the dam, the heart of the republic's future industry and irrigation, depends on their effort.

6.name: Stalinobodiyon
6.text:
The Men of Stalinabad are the old cadres of the party, police and procuracy who served when Dushanbe still bore Stalin's name, a name removed in 1961. Many fought in the war or in the campaigns against the Basmachi and religion, and since Khrushchev's fall they have regained their voice in district committees and veterans' councils.

They want iron discipline, harsh treatment of mullahs and nationalists, a restored respect for Stalin and unconditional obedience to Moscow. They despise the poets of the Thaw and the regional clans alike, and see America and China as enemies. Their leverage is experience in repression, the security organs and allies among Moscow's conservatives.

7.name: Kumitai Amniyati Davlatii RSS Tojikiston
7.text:
The KGB of the Tajik SSR is the republican arm of the Committee for State Security, answering to Yuri Andropov in Moscow. Guarding the long border with Afghanistan and China along the Panj and the Pamirs, it also watches over the uranium works of Leninabad province and the foreign guests who visit Dushanbe.

It stands for vigilance: informers in every kolkhoz and institute, pressure on unregistered mullahs and underground hujras, and surveillance of Ismaili contacts with the Aga Khan. Loyal first to Moscow, it keeps files on the Tajik elite as well. Its leverage is secrecy, the border troops and the fear its name inspires.

8.name: Jamoati ismoiliyoni Badakhshon
8.text:
The Ismaili Community of Badakhshan unites the Nizari Ismaili Shia of the Pamir valleys of Gorno-Badakhshan, whose spiritual leader is the Aga Khan IV, imam since 1957 and living in Europe. Cut off from him by the Soviet border, the community in 1970 survives through family devotion, secret prayer houses and the memory of its missionaries.

It stands for an open, rational faith that prizes education, the equality of women, peaceful coexistence and loyalty to the state in which it lives. It seeks no power but longs for contact with the imam. Its leverage is the high education of Pamiris and the community's strong sense of solidarity.

9.name: Khalifahoi Pomir
9.text:
The Khalifas of the Pamir are the hereditary religious leaders and pir families of the Ismaili valleys of Shughnan, Rushan, Ishkashim and Wakhan. Stripped of their lands and offices after 1917, they still lead funerals, recitations and secret rites in 1970, and villagers still bring them tithes in kind.

They hold that the community must be guided by its religious hierarchy rather than by Soviet officials or secular intellectuals, and they reject atheism, collectivised morals and the Russian schools that weaken the faith. They are hostile to Moscow but have no foreign sponsor. Their leverage is sacred lineage, ritual authority and the loyalty of the remote mountain villages.

10.name: Qoziyoti musulmononi Tojikiston
10.text:
The Qaziate of Tajikistan is the republican office in Dushanbe of the Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of Central Asia and Kazakhstan, the state-recognised muftiate headed in Tashkent by Mufti Ziyauddin Babakhanov. In 1970 it oversees only a few registered mosques for a population that remains deeply believing.

It teaches a loyal Hanafi Islam that accepts Soviet authority, condemns unlicensed mullahs and shrine cults, and praises Soviet peace policy before Muslim delegations from abroad. It works under the control of the Council for Religious Affairs. Its leverage is legitimacy: the only legal imams and the official voice of Islam in the republic.

11.name: Tolibi hujra
11.text:
The Hujra Students are the most radical pupils of the clandestine religious schools of the Vakhsh valley, Kurgan-Tyube and Dushanbe, young men who have learned Arabic and the Quran in back rooms and secretly read imported Arabic pamphlets. In 1970 they are still a scattered handful, unknown even to most of their neighbours.

They reject their teachers' quietism and the official muftiate, call Soviet rule infidel and dream of an Islamic state under sharia from the Pamirs to the Fergana Valley. They are hostile to Moscow and to the West alike. Their leverage is secrecy, zeal and the deep piety of the villages resettled from Gharm and Karategin.

12.name: Halqai Nuri
12.text:
Nuri's Circle gathers young believers around Said Abdullo Nuri, a twenty-two-year-old from a Karategin family resettled in the Vakhsh valley, who studies religion privately with underground teachers including Muhammadjan Hindustani. On 1 January 1970 it is an informal group of friends who meet to study, pray and discuss the state of Muslims.

They want Islam restored to public life through education, preaching and moral renewal rather than violence, and dream of a society where faith and modern learning go together. They oppose Soviet atheism but are wary of foreign powers. Their leverage is youthful energy, kinship networks among the Gharmi resettlers and the hunger for religious knowledge.

13.name: Leninobodiyon
13.text:
The Leninabad Clan is the network of party and state officials from the northern province of Leninabad around Khujand, which has supplied the republic's leaders since the 1940s. First Secretary Jabbor Rasulov is its patron, and its members dominate the Central Committee, the Council of Ministers and the economic ministries.

It seeks stability, northern primacy and a steady flow of investment, trading loyal cotton and plan fulfilment for freedom from Moscow's interference. It has no ideology beyond keeping power, and regards Kulob, Gharm and the Pamirs as junior partners. Its leverage is control of appointments, the industrial north and long-standing ties to Moscow and Tashkent.

14.name: Hujrai Hindustoni
14.text:
Hindustani's Hujra is the underground teaching circle of Muhammadjan Hindustani, a Kokand-born scholar trained in British India who returned to Central Asia, survived the Gulag and now lives in Dushanbe. In private homes he teaches Arabic, Hanafi law and Persian classics to a stream of pupils from across Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.

He preaches a conservative, apolitical Islam: patience under Soviet rule, loyalty to the Hanafi tradition and the local saints, and rejection of both atheism and imported Arab radicalism. He shuns politics and foreign alignments. His leverage is the authority of knowledge, a growing chain of students and the respect of believers who see him as the last great teacher.

15.name: Leninabadskiy gorno-khimicheskiy kombinat
15.text:
The Leninabad Mining and Chemical Combine at Chkalovsk is the plant that produced the Soviet Union's first uranium concentrate in 1945 and still runs mines and mills across northern Tajikistan. It belongs to the secret Ministry of Medium Machine Building, not to Dushanbe, and its closed town has its own shops, salaries and police.

Its directors want investment, secrecy and freedom from republican interference, and serve the nuclear rivalry with the United States above all else. They care little for local politics. Their leverage is strategic material for the bomb, Moscow budgets and the best-paid jobs in the republic.

16.name: Bozori Panjshanbe
16.text:
The Panjshanbe Bazaar stands for the traders of Leninabad's great Thursday market and the private dealers of the Tajik towns who keep the grey economy alive. Dried fruit, silk, carpets, livestock and deficit goods from Tashkent and beyond change hands through networks of relatives, bribes and trust.

They want freedom to buy, sell and keep the profit, more room for household plots and an end to raids by the economic police. They care little for ideology and admire Western goods more than Western ideas. Their leverage is that families and officials alike depend on what only the bazaar can supply.

17.name: Beshai Palangon
17.text:
The Tigrovaya Balka Nature Reserve was founded in 1938 in the tugai forests of the lower Vakhsh to protect the last refuge of the Turan tiger, which has not been seen there since the 1950s. In 1970 its biologists and their colleagues in the Tajik Academy of Sciences form the core of the republic's conservation movement.

They warn against the drainage of the river forests for cotton, against pesticides, and against the ecological cost of the Vakhsh dams, and they call for protection of the Bukhara deer and mountain wildlife. They work within the Soviet system and avoid protest. Their leverage is scientific authority and growing public affection for the reserve.

18.name: Pakhtakoroni Vakhsh
18.text:
The Vakhsh Cotton Growers are the kolkhoz workers and brigade leaders of the irrigated south, many of them mountain families forcibly resettled from Gharm, Karategin and Kulob to the cotton plains. In 1970 they produce most of the republic's cotton while living in poor villages with few schools or clinics.

They want collective farming that serves the farmers: higher procurement prices, less forced labour for children and students at harvest time, clean water and investment in rural services. They are loyal to Soviet socialism and indifferent to foreign blocs. Their leverage is that the cotton plan, and with it the republic's standing in Moscow, depends on their hands.

19.name: Shotemuriyon
19.text:
Shotemur's Heirs are intellectuals and younger party members who honour Shirinsho Shotemur and Nusratullo Maksum, the founders of Soviet Tajikistan who fought for a separate republic in 1929 and were shot in 1937. Rehabilitated after Stalin's death, their memory inspires historians and teachers in Dushanbe.

They are convinced communists who want real sovereignty for the Tajik republic: native cadres, Tajik-language education, development of industry rather than cotton monoculture and an honest history of the 1920s and 1930s. They reject capitalism and Uzbek or Russian hegemony alike. Their leverage lies in the Academy of Sciences, the universities and the sympathy of many officials.

20.name: Samarqand va Bukhoro
20.text:
Samarkand and Bukhara is the populist grievance that the two great centres of Persian-speaking civilisation were handed to Uzbekistan in the national delimitation of 1924, leaving the Tajiks with mountains and villages. In 1970 it cannot be said in public, but it is repeated at every family table in Dushanbe and the north.

Its supporters demand recognition of the Tajik character of Samarkand and Bukhara, Tajik schools there, protection from Uzbek dominance and priority for Tajiks in jobs and housing. They distrust Tashkent and Moscow alike. Their leverage is national resentment and the sympathy of officials who share it.

21.name: Lashkari Ibrohimbek
21.text:
The Army of Ibrahim Bek is the legend and the last veterans of the Basmachi commander who fought Soviet rule in eastern Bukhara for a decade and was executed in 1932. His kinsmen and followers live on in the Lakai villages of the south and among émigrés in northern Afghanistan, watched closely by the KGB.

Their ideal is a militarised, ethnically defined state under warrior chiefs, purged of Russians and communists and ruled by the sword and custom. Fiercely anti-Soviet, they hope for any war that might weaken Moscow. Their leverage is a legend of resistance and blood ties across the Afghan border.

22.name: 201-ya motostrelkovaya diviziya
22.text:
The 201st Motor Rifle Division, which earned its Gatchina honorific in the war, has been stationed in Dushanbe since the end of the Second World War and is the main Soviet ground force in the Tajik SSR. Since 1969 it belongs to the new Central Asian Military District, facing China in the Pamirs and watching the Afghan border.

Its officers demand priority for the frontier, discipline over clan politics and modern equipment for mountain warfare. They are loyal to the Soviet leadership but impatient with civilian officials. Their leverage is armed force in the capital and Moscow's concern for the security of the southern border.

23.name: Sulolai Manghitiyon
23.text:
The Manghit dynasty ruled the Emirate of Bukhara, including most of today's Tajikistan, until the Red Army stormed Bukhara in 1920. The last emir, Alim Khan, fled to Dushanbe and then to Kabul, where he died in 1944; in 1970 his descendants live in Afghanistan, Turkey and beyond.

The house stands for an Islamic monarchy based on sharia, the authority of the ulama and the old Bukharan order, and it regards Soviet rule as illegitimate. Its exiled members lean towards anti-communist governments but lack any real backing. Its leverage is dynastic legitimacy and the nostalgia of Bukharan émigrés.
